title: Solitude in the crowd
hookLine: Naqshbandi Sufis keep a silent remembrance going while living ordinary lives

cards: A market at noon. Carts, voices, prices called across the stalls, someone haggling over a roll of cloth. In the middle of it a merchant is doing ordinary business: weighing, counting, smiling at a regular customer.

And inside, silently, without a word on his lips, he is remembering God. Nobody around him can tell. That scene is the picture behind a short Persian phrase that Naqshbandi Sufis keep close: khalwat dar anjuman.

teach.h: OUTWARDLY WITH PEOPLE, INWARDLY WITH GOD.
teach.b: The Naqshbandi order is one of the Sufi paths, named for Baha al-Din Naqshband.
Its teachers kept a handful of short Persian phrases as signposts, and solitude in the crowd is one of them: outwardly with people, inwardly with God.

teach.h: THE HAND AT WORK, THE HEART WITH THE FRIEND.
teach.b: A saying handed down in the order puts it even more simply: the hand at work, the heart with the Friend.
You met dhikr, remembrance, on day two hundred sixty-nine. The Naqshbandi way puts its weight on the silent kind, dhikr of the heart, rather than remembrance said aloud.

So a Naqshbandi can trade, cook, raise children, ride a crowded train, and keep the remembrance running underneath, unheard. Beside this phrase the order keeps others just as short. Awareness in the breath.
Watch your step, eyes on where your feet are going. A journey inside your own homeland. Together they describe a path that doesn't need a cave.
The Qur'an gives a picture of it, in Pickthall's translation: "Men whom neither merchandise nor sale beguileth from remembrance of Allah." The merchandise is still there. So is the sale.
What changes is whether it pulls the heart away.
Other Sufis go off into retreat, away from everyone, and tomorrow is about that.
The Naqshbandi phrase doesn't throw retreat out. It carries it into the street.

how: Naqshbandi Sufis are taught a silent remembrance of the heart, kept up through work and family life, guided by short Persian principles such as solitude in the crowd and awareness in the breath.

games.q: what does “solitude in the crowd” mean?
o: a monk's cell built in the middle of a city
a prayer said aloud together in a crowded mosque
silent remembrance kept up in everyday busy life

games.q: solitude in the crowd: tap the pairs.

s: solitude in the crowd means you must leave town to practice
it carries the retreat into the street: outwardly with people, inwardly with God.
the Naqshbandi way puts its weight on silent remembrance
dhikr of the heart, kept running underneath an ordinary day.
in the Qur'an verse, the market disappears
merchandise and sale are still there. what matters is whether they pull the heart from remembrance.

games.q: you're a Naqshbandi with a stall in a busy market. the noon crowd is loud. what does solitude in the crowd ask of you?
o: close the stall and go find a quiet cave.
keep trading, with silent remembrance running underneath.
call out your remembrance over the noise.
games.why: the hand at work, the heart with the Friend. the market goes on; the remembrance runs silently beneath it.

practice: Listen for the sounds of other people, voices, traffic, a door down the hall, a television somewhere, and don't shut them out; let them be the market around you.
Underneath, keep one quiet thing going: if you pray, a silent word of remembrance carried on the breath, and if you don't, simply the breath itself, noticed in and out.

wordCard.voice: Solitude in the crowd. In Persian, khalwat dar anjuman: a Naqshbandi Sufi phrase for silent remembrance kept up in the middle of ordinary life. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: solitude in the gathering; one of the Naqshbandi order's short guiding phrases.

carryVoice: Your line: alone in the crowd. The solitude is real; it just doesn't need an empty room. Same time tomorrow.
